headline: Democrats sweep the US midterms, the RBA hikes rates to an 18-year high, and your US tech stocks (MSFT +6.6%, GOOG +4.8%, TTWO +5.8%) had a massive night — but the ASX slipped on the rate news.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft smashed last night's session, jumping 6.6% after blowout FY27 Q1 earnings showed its AI cloud business (Azure) is growing faster than Wall Street expected. The market is rewarding Microsoft for winning the enterprise AI race — analysts now see it as the clear leader in AI spending among the big tech hyperscalers. Your position is now up 25% overall.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two surged 5.8% last night as GTA VI hype hit fever pitch — pre-loading has been moved up to November 10th and the 212GB download size is making headlines. Analysts are increasingly tipping GTA VI to be one of the biggest-selling games ever. The stock is still slightly below your cost base overall, but the near-term GTA VI catalyst is very real.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet bounced 4.8% last night, recovering from a recent sell-off after earnings showed slower Search growth and a Gemini-related lawsuit spooked investors. The recovery was partly driven by Google unveiling the Gemini 4 Carbon model — benchmark results show it's the least likely frontier AI model to hallucinate, narrowly beating Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. Still down about 5% on your overall investment though.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped 1.6% today as the ASX AI sector absorbed some jitters around the Democrats' midterm win, with analysts flagging that stronger AI regulation is now more likely in the US. One Saxo strategist called it 'a higher hurdle, not an extinction event' for AI stocks. The ETF is down about 19% overall — the AI theme is intact long-term, but the regulatory headwind is real.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara slipped another 1.1% today, adding to a rough run. Citi cut its lithium price forecasts this week citing growing concerns about battery demand, and analysts are lowering long-term assumptions for lithium miners. The stock is down over 61% from your cost base — the structural lithium demand story is intact for the long term, but the near-term headwinds are significant.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE dipped 0.55% today, tracking general emerging markets softness. No major single catalyst — broad caution around the Iran conflict and global rate outlook is weighing on riskier markets generally. Down 8% on your overall investment.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG eased 0.53% at today's close, dragged by the broader ASX dip following the RBA rate hike news. Nothing fundamentally wrong here — this is a diversified fund holding thousands of global companies, and a small daily dip in a rising-rate environment is totally normal noise.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS barely moved today, slipping just 0.19%. It tracks the entire US share market, so last night's big tech rally (MSFT, GOOG) will likely flow through more clearly when US markets open tonight. Your position is up 2.5% overall.

movers.name: DHHF.AX
movers.note: DHHF was essentially flat today, down just 0.19%. This broadly diversified fund tracks global shares and is a core long-term hold — slight daily moves like this are completely normal and not worth reading into.

watch_today.title: RBA hikes to 18-year high — mortgage pain continues
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate again this week to its highest level in 18 years, with big banks already passing on the full increase to variable rate mortgages. The RBA warned inflation will sting for another year yet — but crucially, the vote was split, suggesting a pause could be coming. If you have a home loan, budget for higher repayments. For your portfolio, higher rates weigh on growth stocks and ETFs like VDHG in the short term, but don't change the long-term case.

watch_today.title: MSFT — earnings smash, hold and enjoy the ride
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped 6.6% last night after blowout Q1 FY27 results showing Azure AI cloud growth well ahead of expectations. Your MSFT position is now up 25% overall. This is exactly what long-term buy-and-hold looks like — no action needed, just sit tight and let it compound.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA VI pre-load moved up, hold ahead of launch
watch_today.detail: Take-Two surged 5.8% last night as GTA VI pre-loading was brought forward to November 10th. The game is shaping up to be a generational release. Your position is still slightly below cost base, but the GTA VI launch catalyst is imminent. Hold firm — this is exactly the moment long-term investors were patient for.

watch_today.title: PLS — lithium headwinds persist, but hold for the long term
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals slipped again today and is down over 61% from your cost base. Citi has cut lithium price forecasts citing weaker-than-expected battery demand. This is painful, but the structural case for lithium in the energy transition is a decade-long story. Selling now locks in a big loss at the bottom of the cycle. Hold unless your conviction in the long-term thesis has changed.

watch_today.title: GXAI — Democratic midterms mean tighter AI regulation ahead
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF dipped 1.6% today as markets priced in a higher chance of US AI regulation following the Democrats' midterm sweep. Analysts say this is a headwind, not a death knell, for the AI sector. The long-term case for AI remains strong. Hold — but be aware regulatory risk is now a real factor to watch over the next 12 months.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Gemini 4 Carbon is a genuine AI milestone, consider topping up
watch_today.detail: Alphabet bounced 4.8% last night after releasing Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier AI model that benchmarks show is the least likely of any major AI to hallucinate (make things up). It narrowly beat Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. Your GOOG position is still marginally below cost (-5%). If you've been thinking about adding more, the combination of the recent dip and this product breakthrough makes this a reasonable moment for a long-term top-up.

world.summary: The two biggest global stories right now: Democrats have won the US midterm elections in what's being called a landslide, reshaping the political landscape for the next two years — and there's a live war between the US and Iran, with both sides now reportedly reviewing peace proposals.

stories.title: Democrats win US midterms in a landslide — Republicans blame Trump
stories.why_it_matters: Democrats have swept the 2026 US midterm elections in what multiple outlets are calling a 'blue tsunami,' flipping control of Congress away from Republicans. Angry Republicans are publicly blaming Donald Trump for the defeat, with one calling it 'a disaster.' Trump himself has said in an interview he will accept the election results. For global markets, a Democratic-controlled Congress means tighter AI regulation is now more likely and some of Trump's economic agenda could be blocked — though analysts note it's a 'higher hurdle, not an extinction event' for US tech and AI stocks.

stories.title: US-Iran war: peace proposals on the table as conflict grinds on
stories.why_it_matters: The US and Iran are actively reviewing proposals to end their ongoing war, according to Bloomberg — but Iran is playing down hopes for a quick deal after fresh US airstrikes on the eve of the midterm elections. Israel has also reportedly told US and Gulf allies that Iran is planning to use chemical weapons. The Strait of Hormuz — a critical chokepoint for global oil supply — remains a flashpoint. Oil dropped 2.3% last night to $93.91/barrel, suggesting markets are cautiously pricing in some chance of de-escalation, though the conflict remains extremely dangerous.

stories.title: Trump says he'll accept election results, but warns of executive powers
stories.why_it_matters: Donald Trump has told interviewers he will accept the midterm election results — a notable statement given his history around the 2020 election. However, analysts and commentators are flagging that Trump may lean heavily on presidential executive powers to pursue his agenda even without a supportive Congress, including potential moves around trade tariffs, immigration, and energy policy. The world is watching closely how US domestic politics now plays out with a Democratic legislature acting as a check on the White House.

stories.title: Gold hits record highs as global uncertainty spikes
stories.why_it_matters: Gold jumped 2.6% last night to $4,042 USD per ounce — a remarkable level reflecting genuine investor anxiety about the Iran war, the US political situation, and sticky global inflation. Gold is a classic 'fear trade' — when people are worried about geopolitical instability or currency debasement, they pile into gold. The World Gold Council has actually slightly lowered its demand growth outlook due to slowing bar buying, but investment demand from institutions and central banks remains strong.

stories.title: Democrats' win raises AI regulation fears for tech stocks
stories.why_it_matters: US tech stocks initially sold off then partially recovered after the Democratic midterms sweep, as investors weighed up what a more regulation-friendly Congress means for AI companies. Democrats are more likely to push through meaningful AI regulation, which could slow deployment and increase compliance costs for companies like Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Asian chip stocks also fell on the news. However, one Saxo strategist put it well: this is 'a higher hurdle, not an extinction event' — the AI gold rush continues, just with more rules around it.

markets.summary: Last night was a big night for US markets — the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both surged strongly on the back of tech earnings (Microsoft in particular) and some relief around the US election outcome. The ASX pulled back today, dragged by the RBA rate hike. Oil fell on cautious Iran war optimism, while gold surged to over $4,000 on geopolitical fear.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: The Aussie market slipped 0.59% today, with rate-sensitive sectors under pressure after the RBA hiked rates to an 18-year high.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night the S&P jumped 1.69%, driven by strong tech earnings — Microsoft's blowout result was the standout catalyst.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night the NASDAQ surged 2.25% — tech's biggest single-night move in weeks, with AI-linked names leading the charge.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil dropped 2.3% last night as markets cautiously priced in a small chance of US-Iran peace talks bearing fruit.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold surged 2.6% to over $4,000 — investors are piling into safe-haven assets amid the Iran war and global political uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat, trading at 70.1 US cents. The RBA hike provided a tiny lift but it's not moving much.

politics.summary: The RBA has hiked interest rates to an 18-year high, big banks are passing it straight on to mortgage holders, and Treasurer Jim Chalmers is in damage control mode — insisting the government isn't to blame while the AFR and opposition say Labor's economic model is broken.

stories.title: RBA hikes rates to 18-year high — big banks immediately follow
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia lifted the cash rate again, pushing it to its highest level in 18 years. Australia's big banks moved quickly to pass on the full increase to variable rate mortgage customers — 'Friday the 13th horror for homeowners' as one headline put it. The RBA warned that inflation will continue hurting Australians for at least another year. However, the board vote was split, which Reuters says 'points to a pause ahead' — so this may be close to the peak.

stories.title: Chalmers fires back: 'I'm not the Broncos waterboy'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers pushed back hard on criticism that Labor's spending is fuelling inflation and forcing the RBA's hand. In a fiery exchange, Chalmers said he promises to be 'helpful' on inflation but rejected any blame for the rate hike, reportedly saying 'I'm not the Broncos waterboy' in response to suggestions he should simply do what the RBA tells him. The AFR's headline today was blunt: 'Labor's economic model is broken and households are paying the bill.' The political pressure on Labor over cost-of-living is intensifying.

stories.title: Gas policy consultants worked for industry and government simultaneously
stories.why_it_matters: An ABC News investigation has found that consultants advising the Australian government on gas policy were simultaneously working for the gas industry — a classic conflict of interest story. The government has been leaning heavily on consultants to shape energy market policy, and this raises serious questions about whose interests were actually being served when those policies were written. It's another headache for Labor at a time when energy costs are front of mind for households.

stories.title: Australia's social media ban has 'modest effect' on teen political views, government tells court
stories.why_it_matters: In court proceedings around Australia's under-16 social media ban, the government's own submission acknowledged the ban has only a 'modest effect' on teenagers' political communication. Critics argue this undermines the government's justification for such a sweeping law. Meanwhile, a separate inquiry heard that Labor's proposed Digital Duty of Care laws could inadvertently catch legitimate news content in its net — raising concerns about press freedom and the scope of the legislation.

stories.title: Budget 'tough love' could hand Labor election-winning surplus
stories.why_it_matters: An analysis in Independent Australia argues that Labor's willingness to absorb political pain on interest rates and cost-of-living could actually pay off at the next election — if the economy turns and the budget swings into surplus. The theory: voters may forgive the short-term pain if Labor can claim credit for fixing the inflation problem. It's a risky political bet, but one Chalmers appears to be consciously making.

ai.summary: Google unveiled its most capable AI model yet — Gemini 4 Carbon — which benchmarks show hallucinates less than any other frontier AI. Meanwhile the US midterms are reshaping the AI regulation landscape, and the EU's AI Act is now applying in Northern Ireland.

stories.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon: the AI that makes stuff up the least
stories.why_it_matters: Google has released Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model, and benchmarks show it narrowly beats Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 — including being the least likely of any major AI to hallucinate (that is, confidently make up wrong information). For everyday users, this matters because hallucination is the main reason people can't trust AI for serious tasks like medical questions or legal research. A more reliable AI is a more useful AI. This news directly boosted GOOG's share price last night.

stories.title: Democrats' midterm win puts AI regulation firmly on the agenda
stories.why_it_matters: The Democrats' sweeping midterm victory means a Congress that is far more likely to push through meaningful AI regulation — including rules around transparency, data use, and potentially limiting how AI can be deployed in sensitive areas like healthcare, employment, and elections. The US dollar fell slightly on the news as markets recalibrated. Asian chip stocks also dropped. For investors in AI-linked stocks and ETFs, this is a real headwind but not a reason to panic — the technology is too economically important to be regulated out of existence.

stories.title: AI-powered cyberattacks are getting much harder to stop
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all accelerating their push into cybersecurity as AI-powered cyberattacks become more sophisticated and harder to detect. The same AI tools that make software smarter are also making hacking faster and more automated — meaning security teams are now racing against AI-generated threats. This is driving serious investment in AI security competition, which is a growing commercial opportunity for all three companies.

stories.title: EU AI Act now applies in Northern Ireland
stories.why_it_matters: The EU's AI Act — the world's first comprehensive law regulating artificial intelligence — now formally applies in Northern Ireland due to its unique post-Brexit legal status. The law bans certain high-risk uses of AI (like social scoring and real-time biometric surveillance in public) and requires transparency around AI-generated content. For tech companies selling AI products in Europe, compliance costs are rising. Australia is watching closely and may eventually follow with its own framework.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — the Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Off-season NRL signings are heating up, AFL clubs are making moves, and tennis is in full swing at the Rolex Paris Masters.

stories.title: NRL Grand Final: Roosters beat Knights 19-18 in a classic
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters are premiers after defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a one-point Grand Final thriller at Accor Stadium. It was as close as it gets — one point separating the two sides at the final whistle. A massive result for the Roosters and a heartbreaking end for the Knights, who came so close to their first premiership in years.

stories.title: Bears eye Tom Burton with $6m salary cap exemption weapon
stories.why_it_matters: The North Sydney Bears are reportedly using a $6 million marquee player salary cap exemption as their headline weapon to lure star player Tom Burton away from his current club. The marquee exemption allows clubs to sign elite players outside the normal salary cap limits, giving the Bears a genuine financial advantage in the race for his signature. Big off-season move if they pull it off.

stories.title: Gold Coast Titans unveil 11 train-and-trial players for NRL deals
stories.why_it_matters: Your local team, the Gold Coast Titans, have named 11 train-and-trial players who are fighting for NRL contracts heading into the pre-season. These are fringe players who get a chance to prove themselves in trial matches and training — the club is clearly looking to build depth across the squad. Worth keeping an eye on as the 2027 squad starts to take shape.

stories.title: Musetti knocks out World No. 1 Zverev at Rolex Paris Masters
stories.why_it_matters: Italian Lorenzo Musetti has pulled off a big upset at the Rolex Paris Masters, knocking out World No. 1 Alexander Zverev. It's the kind of result that shakes up the year-end rankings and signals that Musetti is genuine title contention. The Paris Masters is one of the final big events before the ATP Finals, so every match has ranking implications at this stage of the season.

stories.title: AFL: North Melbourne sign trio including former top-five draft pick
stories.why_it_matters: North Melbourne have signed three players in their off-season recruitment push, including a former top-five draft pick. The Roos are rebuilding aggressively after a tough few years, and landing a highly-drafted player signals they're serious about competing sooner rather than later. No specific names confirmed yet in the available data, but it's a notable move in the AFL trade and signing period.
